about: Planting and farming data for the Sphere's farm layer and the Pattern Garden, Washington. Every window in this file carries the source it came from. Spring windows are counted in weeks from the county's average last spring frost, the way the almanac and extension calendars count them. Fall windows are the WSU Extension Snohomish County chart's own words; where a machine date is given beside the words, it is the plain reading of those words (mid-July reads as July 15) and the words govern. Where sources disagree, the disagreement is written into the crop's notes rather than smoothed over. A crop or window with no sourced value is left out, never guessed. The county set stands at all thirty-nine Washington counties (entered Nov 20, 2026): every county is anchored on its real frost record — a named NOAA 1991–2020 normals station for its garden ground, or, for the one county with no station of its own, a computed entry that says so and names its anchors and its rule. Each county entry carries its provenance — published or computed — and a county's safe line follows the garden's stated safe rule where no published safe line was entered. Frost-free days are the station's published season length; NOAA counts the season from unrounded values, so it can differ by a few days from the gap between the rounded median dates printed in an entry.

crops.name: Tomatoes
notes: Two sources count the indoor start differently: WSU's Pacific Northwest Gardener's Handbook allows 5–6 weeks from seed to transplant size, the Farmer's Almanac cohort is 6–8 weeks. The window here (5–8) holds both.

The transplant time is WSU's western Washington rule — soil warmth, mid-May — and deliberately does not follow the county frost count. Nurseries stock tomatoes in April; WSU says that is far too early to put them in the ground here.

fixed.label: mid-May, once the soil is at 50°F or warmer

crops.name: Peppers
notes: WSU times peppers by soil warmth and publishes no calendar date for western Washington. The window here is the extension class rule for very tender crops (2 or more weeks after the last frost); in a cold spring, wait for warm soil even inside the window.

crops.name: Basil
notes: WSU publishes no sourced western Washington calendar date for basil; the timing here is the Farmer's Almanac late-starter cohort plus the very-tender class rule, and it is labeled as such.

crops.name: Bush Beans
notes: WSU's bean guidance times sowing by soil at 65°F and gives no calendar date. The window here is the Almanac's sow-at-the-last-frost rule; in a cold spring, wait for the soil inside the window.

crops.name: Cucumbers
notes: Do not let cucurbit transplants get root-bound; WSU's gardener's handbook warns they can be permanently stunted. Direct sowing is the safer road here.

crops.name: Melons (cantaloupe)
notes: Western Washington summers are cool for melons; the window is the extension class rule, and a warm spot decides more than the calendar does.

fall.text: Sow mid-July, for fall and winter harvest

crops.name: Carrots
notes: Sources place carrots differently: the Farmer's Almanac lists them among crops sown 4–6 weeks before the last frost, while the extension class table counts them semi-hardy at 0–2 weeks before. The earlier window is shown; the class table's later window also grows carrots here, just later.

fall.text: Sow before August, for fall and winter harvest; beet greens only, through September 1

crops.name: Beets
notes: As with carrots, the Almanac's early window (4–6 weeks before the last frost) is shown; the extension class table counts beets semi-hardy at 0–2 weeks before.

fall.text: Sow until mid-September, for fall harvest; winter radish varieties are planted in July and harvested all winter
Sow by mid-August; for greens, plant through September

crops.name: Parsnips
notes: A light frost brings out the best flavor in parsnips (WSU Snohomish fall chart); they are often left in the ground and dug through winter.

fall.text: Seed until mid-July for fall use; seedlings made in August usually winter over for spring use. Onion sets can be planted any time in fall and winter if the soil is drained and workable

notes: Three WSU voices give three shades of the same answer: the Snohomish fall chart says 'late fall', WSU's garlic guide puts western Washington planting in November, and a Skagit County WSU article says October. The October–November window holds all three rather than picking one.

locations.anchor: Morton–Centralia lowland, and the Randle valley floor
locations.frostRangeNote: Two honest answers exist for this county's frost dates, and both are kept. The NOAA median (the middle year of 1991–2020) says last spring frost Apr 22 and first fall frost Oct 27. The Old Farmer's Almanac, counting a 30% chance of frost after the date instead, says Apr 30 and Oct 19. The median plans the season; the Almanac line is the safer one for tender plants.

provenance.basis: Median dates are the Centralia station's NOAA 1991–2020 normals; the safe line is the Old Farmer's Almanac's published 30% reading of the same station — both entered from their publications, not computed.

locations.anchor: Yakima and the valley floor
locations.frostRangeNote: Yakima's city station speaks for the valley floor. The county's benches and side valleys run later: Wapato Apr 21 – Oct 15, Sunnyside May 1 – Oct 6, Selah May 5 – Oct 4. The floor is the warm heart; gardens climb colder from it.

sources.name: The garden's safe line, stated as a rule rather than a measurement: for a county whose safe dates were not themselves published, the safe spring date stands ten days after the median last frost and the safe fall date ten days before the median first frost. The founded counties keep their own published safe lines — Lewis the Almanac's 30% reading (Apr 30 / Oct 19 at Centralia), Snohomish WSU's observed latest (May 1 / Oct 4) — and the ten-day rule stands in the same spirit for the rest.

The garden's computed-county rule, stated rather than measured: where no NOAA 1991–2020 normals station stands in a county, the county's median dates are computed from the named anchor stations in the same river valley — their median spring and fall dates averaged, then shifted one day later in spring and one day earlier in fall for each 250 ft the county's garden ground stands above the anchors' mean elevation (the reverse below it), rounded to the nearest day. A computed entry says so in its provenance and is never presented as a station's record.
